lead: A fork is a split in the block chain: two histories that share a parent but not the same future. Forks happen when software rules change, when a bug is fixed, when developers or miners disagree, and even in normal operation when two miners find a block at the same height. The label soft or hard depends on one test: do nodes running the old rules still accept blocks made under the new rules? That test decides whether the network stays on one chain or splits into two coins.
prereq: You need: 3.4 and 3.5 for the two ways blocks are produced, and Unit 1 for block structure and hash links.

sections.h3: What a fork is, and the ordinary temporary fork

blocks.text: A fork is any divergence in the block chain: two blocks or two chains with a shared parent. One cause is ordinary latency. Miner A and miner B may find a block at the same height, both with parent at height 100. Some nodes hear A first, some hear B. The next block, mined on one of them, makes the other a stale block: a valid block that is not in the best chain. Nodes then reorganise to the heavier chain. Reorg depth is the number of blocks removed from the best chain in that switch. This temporary fork is normal and does not change the rules. Rule-change forks are different: a software upgrade, a bug fix that changes validity, disagreement among developers or miners, or an emergency rollback. The fork type is decided by validity, not by who intends what.

sections.h3: Soft fork: tighter rules, old nodes still accept

blocks.text: A soft fork tightens the rules. A block valid under the new rules is also valid under the old rules, so old nodes accept it.

blocks.where: NewValid(B) means block B passes the new rules; OldValid(B) means B passes the old rules. The arrow means: if the left side is true, the right side must also be true.

blocks.text: Some old-valid blocks may fail the new rules; new nodes reject those. That is still backward compatible because the old software can follow the new chain. A soft fork needs a majority of hash power or stake to enforce the tighter rule. If only a minority runs it, old-rule miners can keep producing blocks that new nodes reject, and two tips can compete until one side wins. SegWit in Bitcoin in 2017 is the standard example: it changed how signature data is counted without making old nodes reject the new blocks. A soft fork can therefore split the chain for a while, but it does not require a permanent split.

sections.h3: Hard fork: incompatible rules, permanent split, and confirmation depth

blocks.text: A hard fork widens or changes the rules so that old and new nodes disagree on validity. There is a block B with NewValid(B) true and OldValid(B) false. Old nodes reject B, so they reject the new chain. If a large group keeps running the old rules and mining, the result is two chains with separate histories and separate coins. Bitcoin Cash in 2017 raised the block size and split from Bitcoin. Ethereum's 2016 hard fork reversed the DAO theft; the chain that rejected the change became Ethereum Classic. A hard fork is a rule change, not automatically two live coins: if every node and miner upgrades, the old chain stops. Confirmation depth protects against temporary forks. Waiting for k confirmations means the block holding the transaction has k−1 blocks built on top of it. The transaction survives only if the reorg depth is less than k. The chance that a shorter branch overtakes it falls as k grows. Reorg depth measures how many blocks were replaced. A stale block is one discarded block under the same rules, not a hard fork.

examples.question: At height 100 the network splits. Miners on the new rules have 85% of total hash power; old-rule miners have 15%. Ignore difficulty changes and network latency. (a) When the new chain has mined 2016 blocks, what is its height? (b) What is the expected number of old-chain blocks in the same time, rounded to the nearest whole block? (c) What is the old-chain height?
steps: The new chain mines 2016 blocks, so its height is 100 + 2016 = 2116.
The old-to-new block rate ratio is 0.15 ÷ 0.85 = 3/17 = 0.17647.
Expected old-chain blocks = 2016 × 0.17647 = 355.76 blocks. A block count is an integer, so round to 356 blocks.

This count assumes difficulty stays fixed, as the question states. In a real split each chain retargets its own difficulty; the old chain's difficulty falls with its hash power, its block rate rises, and the old-chain count in the same time would be larger than 356.
examples.answer: The new chain is at height 2116, the old chain is expected to have 355.76 blocks (356 whole blocks), so the old chain is at height 456.

old_share = 0.15
new_share = 0.85
old_blocks = new_blocks * old_share / new_share
print(100 + new_blocks)
print(round(old_blocks, 2))
print(round(old_blocks))
print(100 + round(old_blocks))

traps: Saying a soft fork can never split the chain: during activation a minority old-rule chain can compete, and a lasting split is possible if old miners keep mining blocks that new nodes reject.
Calling an ordinary stale block a hard fork: the stale block follows the same rules and is discarded only because another branch grew first.
Assuming a hard fork always creates two live coins: if every node and miner upgrades, the old chain stops and no second coin survives.
Reversing backward compatibility: a soft fork means old software accepts new blocks, not that new software accepts every old block.
Treating confirmations as a formality: each extra confirmation lowers the chance that a temporary fork reverses the transaction.

quiz.q: Define a soft fork in one sentence.
quiz.a: A soft fork is a rule change that tightens validity, so every block valid under the new rules is still valid under the old rules and old nodes accept it.

quiz.q: Define a hard fork in one sentence.
quiz.a: A hard fork is a rule change that is incompatible with the old rules, so old nodes reject new-rule blocks and the chain can split permanently.

quiz.q: Why is a soft fork called backward compatible?
quiz.a: Old nodes accept new-rule blocks because the new rules are a subset of the old rules. The old software can follow the new chain even though it does not enforce the tighter rule.

quiz.q: New-rule miners have 70% of hash power and old-rule miners have 30%. After the new chain mines 1000 blocks, what is the expected number of old-chain blocks? Round to the nearest block.
quiz.a: Rate ratio = 0.30 ÷ 0.70 = 3/7 ≈ 0.42857. Expected old blocks = 1000 × 0.42857 = 428.57, so 429 blocks.

quiz.q: A transaction has 3 confirmations. A reorg replaces 4 blocks from the tip. Is the transaction still in the best chain?
quiz.a: No. With 3 confirmations the block holding the transaction is third from the tip. A 4-block reorg removes the first four blocks from the tip, and any reorg of depth 3 or more would also remove it, because reorg depth ≥ confirmations means the transaction block is replaced. The transaction must be re-mined or re-included.

quiz.q: Two miners find a block at height 101 with the same parent. The next block is mined on one of them. Is this a hard fork?
quiz.a: No. Both blocks follow the same rules. This is a temporary fork caused by latency; the other block becomes a stale block and the network reorganises to one tip.

quiz.q: Why can a hard fork produce two coins, while a soft fork usually does not?
quiz.a: In a hard fork old nodes reject new-rule blocks, so old-rule miners can keep a separate valid chain with its own history and coin. In a soft fork old nodes accept new-rule blocks, so the old tip loses unless a lasting group keeps mining blocks that new nodes reject.
Reorg depth is the number of blocks removed from the best chain when a competing branch becomes the best chain.

beyond: Not for the exam. In practice forks are managed with activation signaling, replay protection and chain IDs; exchanges and wallets often pause deposits around upgrades. Newer research looks at fork choice, finality and social consensus, because code rules cannot settle which chain a community should value. Search next for 'soft fork activation', 'replay protection' and 'chain reorganization'.
